short: Near-weightlessness in orbit.
definition: The condition inside an orbiting spacecraft, where everything is in free fall together so objects float. Gravity has not vanished, but its effects on flames — above all buoyancy — nearly disappear. EMBER treats ISS and free-flying Cygnus tests as 0 g.

short: Gravity weaker than Earth's but not zero, e.g. the Moon (≈0.17 g) or Mars (≈0.38 g).
definition: Surface gravity on the Moon or Mars. Buoyancy still exists but is weaker, so hot gases rise more slowly. Some tests suggest materials can burn more readily at partial gravity than on Earth because the flame gets fresh oxygen without being cooled by fast buoyant flow.

short: Hot, light gas rising and pulling in fresh air.
definition: On Earth, hot combustion products are lighter than the surrounding air, so they rise and draw fresh air in from below. This gives a candle flame its teardrop shape and supplies it with oxygen. In microgravity buoyancy is absent, so a flame only gets oxygen from diffusion or from fans.

short: Airflow made by fans rather than by buoyancy.
definition: In a spacecraft, air only moves because the ventilation system moves it. Typical local speeds are a few to tens of centimetres per second. Experiments such as BASS, BASS-II and Saffire set this speed deliberately to see how it changes fire behaviour.

short: Flame spreading against the incoming air.
definition: The flame front moves upstream, into the oncoming airflow — like a flame creeping down a match held upright on Earth. These flames tend to be small and steady.

short: Flame spreading in the same direction as the air.
definition: The airflow carries the hot flame over unburned fuel ahead of it, preheating it — like upward burning on Earth. On Earth this is usually the fastest-growing, most dangerous configuration.

short: Airflow so slow the flame starves and goes out.
definition: Below a certain flow speed, oxygen reaches the flame too slowly and heat losses win, so the flame shrinks and extinguishes. BASS-II measured this boundary for a cotton-fiberglass fabric.

short: Airflow so fast it blows the flame away.
definition: At high flow speeds the gas moves past the fuel faster than the chemistry can keep up, so the flame detaches and goes out. Between the quenching and blowoff limits lies the flammable range.

short: The condition at which a flame can no longer survive.
definition: A boundary — in oxygen, pressure, flow speed, fuel size or diluent concentration — beyond which a flame goes out. Different mechanisms set it: too little residence time (kinetic), too much heat loss (radiative), or starvation (quenching).

short: A flame going out because it loses too much heat by glowing.
definition: Large, slow microgravity flames radiate a lot of heat away from soot and hot gases. When those losses outweigh the heat released, the flame extinguishes. It is common in weightlessness and rare on Earth.

short: A faint, low-temperature flame (roughly 500–1000 K).
definition: A combustion mode driven by low-temperature chemistry that gives off very little light. FLEX discovered droplets that kept burning with a cool flame after their visible hot flame had gone out, so a fire can look extinguished while reactions continue.

short: An intermediate flame regime between cool and hot flames.
definition: Ground studies building on FLEX identified a warm flame with a two-part reaction structure that links cool and hot flames.

short: The lowest oxygen level at which a fuel keeps burning.
definition: The minimum oxygen concentration (by volume) that supports burning under stated conditions. FLEX measured it for fuel droplets; the partial-gravity tests measured an upward-spread version (ULOI) for solid materials at different gravity levels.

short: The highest oxygen level at which a material does not propagate a flame.
definition: Used in NASA material screening alongside the limiting oxygen index. The gap between the two brackets the material's flammability limit.

short: NASA's standard upward-burning material flammability test, run in 1 g.
definition: A sample is ignited at the bottom and must not burn more than a set length. Because upward burning is thought to be the worst case on Earth, passing it has been taken as evidence a material is safe in space. Microgravity and partial-gravity experiments test that assumption.

short: A heat-release test that measures how much energy a burning material gives off.
definition: An alternative flammability test that measures heat release rate under an applied radiant heat flux. BRE investigators suggested it may relate more directly to low-gravity burning.

short: How much power a fire gives off, in watts.
definition: Often estimated by oxygen-consumption calorimetry: each gram of oxygen consumed releases about the same amount of heat for most fuels.

short: Fine carbon particles formed in fuel-rich flames.
definition: Soot makes flames yellow and bright, radiates heat and becomes smoke when it escapes. Microgravity flames can be far sootier than the same flames on Earth.

short: The flame size at which a flame starts releasing smoke.
definition: As fuel flow increases, a flame eventually emits soot from its tip. The flame length at that moment measures how sooty a fuel is. SPICE measured smoke points in microgravity.

short: A lower-pressure, oxygen-enriched cabin atmosphere proposed for exploration vehicles.
definition: To shorten spacesuit pre-breathing, some exploration vehicles may run below sea-level pressure with a higher oxygen fraction (for example the 8.2 psia / 34% and 10.2 psia / 26.5% atmospheres named in PSI's BRE objectives). Higher oxygen fraction generally raises flammability.

short: Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentration.
definition: NASA's exposure limit for a contaminant (such as carbon monoxide) over a given time, e.g. 1 hour or 24 hours.

short: Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS.
definition: A sealed ISS facility that contains small flame experiments, controls the chamber atmosphere and records data. FLEX, CFI, ACME and SoFIE ran inside it.

short: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus.
definition: The CIR insert that deploys, ignites and films fuel droplets, used by FLEX, FLEX-2 and CFI.

short: Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS.
definition: An enclosed workstation where crew operate experiments through gloves. BASS, BASS-II, SPICE, SLICE, SAME and Confined Combustion used it.

short: An uncrewed cargo spacecraft.
definition: After Cygnus leaves the ISS it is empty of crew, so the Saffire experiments could safely set large fires inside it before it re-entered the atmosphere.

short: Spacecraft Fire Experiments I–VI.
definition: A series of six large-scale fire experiments run inside departing Cygnus vehicles, from metre-long fabric sheets to thick acrylic in exploration atmospheres.

short: A cotton–fiberglass blend fabric used as a standard test fuel.
definition: About 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass by weight. It burns like cotton but the fiberglass keeps its shape, which makes flame spread easy to measure.

short: Polymethyl methacrylate — acrylic plastic.
definition: A well-characterised plastic used as a reference solid fuel in many combustion experiments, as thin films, slabs, rods and spheres.

short: A facility that creates a few seconds of free fall.
definition: An experiment package is dropped inside a tall shaft, giving seconds of weightlessness. A centrifuge inside the package can create partial gravity (Moon or Mars) during the drop.

short: A chart of which conditions let a material burn.
definition: Typically oxygen level against flow speed (or pressure, or gravity). Tested points are marked burned or extinguished, and the boundary between them is the flammability limit. EMBER's Risk Lens shows these maps.

short: How fuel-rich a flame is.
definition: The ratio of actual fuel-to-oxygen to the ideal (stoichiometric) ratio. Values above 1 mean fuel-rich, which favours carbon monoxide and soot.
